newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO on a roll as $500 billion infotech deal clinched.
newsitem.headline: WTO on a roll as $500 billion infotech deal clinched.

text.p: Trade superpowers and developing nations clinched a sweeping $500 billion deal Wednesday to scrap tariffs in information technology products in a big boost to consumers and manufacturers in the booming industry.
For the average consumer, the deal means cheaper information technology products and personal computers sales, said World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero.
Hailing the pact as a "win-win situation" for computer makers, emerging economies and customers, Ruggiero said it would boost cross-border investment flows and economic growth.
"This pact is very important for emerging markets in terms of opening up their economies, lowering their barriers and the possibility of buying products at a lower price," he said.

A total of 39 countries representing 92.5 percent of the world trade in information technology products committed themselves to the pact, which will cut tariffs on computers, telecommunications products, semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, software, CD-ROMs and scientific instruments by the year 2000.
Analysts said the pact opened the way for a vast expansion of the industry and ambitious future deals.

The deal complements February's World Trade Organisation (WTO) pact to liberalise basic telecommunications trade. Together, they cover business worth more than $1 trillion annually, more than the global trade volume of agriculture, cars or textiles, Ruggiero said.
The two pacts on telecommunications and information technology are also a big boost to the credibility of the fledgling World Trade Organisation .
"We're really on a roll," a smiling Ruggiero said in an interview. "For the WTO, this has been a very big step forward."
The first tariff cuts under the deal, shaped in December at a Singapore meeting of ministers organised by the WTO, must take place in July.
Ruggiero said lower tariffs will cut prices for consumers around the world from Asia to Europe.
Singapore, Hong Kong and Malaysia already have zero duties for most products, and Korea has duties of 8 percent. The European Union has more duties to scrap than the United States and Japan.
But the biggest winners would be consumers in India where tariffs as high as 52 percent will come down to zero under the pact, Ruggiero said.

India also stands to gain because it is a major supplier of applications development and maintenance software services to North America and Britain. Its information technology skills, much in demand in North America, were also expected to benefit.
Trade diplomats said computer giants in the United States, Germany, Japan and South Korea stood to gain from the deal, save tens of millions of dollars and boost overseas earnings.
One last hurdle was cleared when Washington decided not to hold up a deal over its discontent with EU tariffs on certain computer network equipment and multimedia personal computers.

Washington says a reclassification of such products by the EU customs authorities has caused higher duties on its imports in violation of world trade rules and the United States has filed a case against the European Union under the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body.

The 39 participants included the United States, the 15-member European Union, Japan and Canada; Australia; Hong Kong; Iceland; Indonesia; South Korea; Norway; Singapore; Switzerland; Turkey; Costa Rica; the Czech Republic; Estonia; Israel; India; Macau; Malaysia; New Zealand; Romania; the Slovak Republic; Thailand; and the Chinese Taipei custom territory -- Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu.
Two countries initially on board, Panama and Poland, did not sign up because of delays in finishing their timetables, but Ruggiero said they may do so in the coming days.
Two more countries in the 130-member trade watchdog, the Philippines and El Salvador, could join in the near future.
